about.metaDescription: B-59 designs and builds civic software that works—for voter access, courts, administrative processes, and public transparency. We modernize civic infrastructure thoughtfully. Learn our mission, how we work, and why we're named B-59.
about.ogDescription: We design and build civic software that actually works. Democracy isn't something you improvise—it's something you design. Mission, values, and the story behind the name.
about.heading: About <brand></brand>
about.intro1: We design and build civic software that actually works <blue>—</blue> for voter access, courts, administrative processes, and public transparency. We do it with care, conviction, and technical competence, for the long term.
about.intro2: Democracy isn't something you improvise. It's something you design. We help institutions and the people they serve get tools that fit how things really work, not how they look on a slide deck.
about.missionBody: <brand></brand> exists to modernize civic infrastructure thoughtfully, and to do it for the progressive movement: the campaigns, committees, and organizations working to widen access rather than narrow it. We're not here to "disrupt" democracy for its own sake or to build flashy consumer apps. We're here to make the systems that underpin democratic life <blue>—</blue> voting, justice, administration, transparency <blue>—</blue> more trustworthy and usable.
about.howWeWork1: We take responsibility for what we build. We resist hype. We bring a public-interest mindset without the weight of big institutions. Our job is to help you see clearly, decide well, and ship things that last.
about.howWeWork2: We work with leaders and teams who operate in high-stakes, uncertain environments. We help them understand the systems they're in, see where those systems fall short, and make clear, defensible choices when the "right" answer isn't obvious.
about.howWeWork3: We don't chase trends or attention. We aim for clarity, accountability, and results that hold up over time.
about.why1: In 1962, <sub></sub> was pursued off the coast of Cuba by the US Navy. Cut off from communication and operating on faulty assumptions, the crew came close to launching a nuclear weapon. <arkhipov></arkhipov> chose restraint.
about.why2: That single act of judgment changed the world. We took the name to honor him and to remind ourselves: systems fail, information is incomplete, and the most important decisions often happen under stress.
about.believeBody: Being human-centered isn't a design aesthetic. It's a commitment. We build for the people and institutions who depend on these systems, and we do it so the work holds up when it matters.

inspirations.metaDescription: What B-59 aspires to. Audrey Tang went from civic hacker and protester to Taiwan's first digital minister by building better government websites, and met COVID with open data. 18F made US agencies more usable by putting a design perspective in the room, and its shutdown in 2025 did not take its methods with it.
inspirations.ogDescription: Audrey Tang, g0v and Taiwan's open-data COVID response; 18F and the work that outlived its shutdown. The two examples B-59 takes its bearings from.
inspirations.heading: Our Inspirations
inspirations.tang1: In 2012, civic hackers in Taiwan started g0v by taking government websites and building better ones <blue>—</blue> the same data at the same address with one letter changed, and actually usable. Audrey Tang was one of them. In 2014, when the Sunflower Movement occupied the legislature, Tang helped keep the occupation's communications running.
inspirations.tang2: Two years later, Taiwan made Tang its first digital minister. A protester became an institution builder, and the qualification was, in the end, having made a better website. When COVID arrived in 2020, the answer was not an app the public was asked to trust. The government put its numbers and its supply data on the web in the open, and civic hackers had the trackers people actually used running within days.
inspirations.tang3: That is what we aspire to: government applying what consumer technology learned about speed, transparency and trusting the user, for public good <blue>—</blue> and the door into the institution opening because the work was good.
inspirations.eighteenF1: 18F was a team inside the US General Services Administration that, from 2014, sat down with federal agencies and did the unglamorous work: user research, plain language, a shared design system, open source by default. Agencies got more usable not through a grand modernization but because someone with a design perspective was in the room when the decisions got made.
inspirations.eighteenF2: On March 1, 2025, it was shut down overnight. The staff were locked out of their computers at midnight.
inspirations.eighteenF3: Almost none of what made 18F work went with them. The methods were published. The design system is open source. The guides are on the web. The team was shut down; the work did not have to stop <blue>—</blue> it needed people willing to keep doing it, at whatever scale they could.
inspirations.take1: Take what consumer software has learned about clarity, speed and respect for the person on the other side of the screen, and spend it on the systems people cannot opt out of: registering to vote, showing up for a shift, finding out what the rules are.
inspirations.take2: Taiwan's trackers were built by a handful of people in a few days. 18F's best work was usually one designer in one meeting. Scale was never the point. Being in the room was.

solutionsReady2vote.metaDescription: ready2vote is a civic product built by B-59. It helps Texans complete their voter registration application online and have it mailed to their county. ready2vote doesn't register you—your county does that when they receive your application. Visit readyto.vote.
solutionsReady2vote.ogDescription: Built by B-59. The first online tool that helps Texans complete their voter registration application and have it mailed to their county. Visit readyto.vote.
solutionsReady2vote.intro1: <r2v></r2v> is the first online tool built to do one thing: help Texans complete their voter registration application on the web and have it mailed to their county for them.
solutionsReady2vote.intro2: In Texas, there's no single “click to register” option run by the state. To get on the voter rolls, you have to get a signed registration application to your county <blue>—</blue> usually by printing a form, filling it out, and mailing it yourself. <r2v></r2v> lets you complete that application online and sign electronically; it then works with a trusted mailing service to print and mail the form to the right county office. You get a copy for your records and can check that it was sent.
solutionsReady2vote.disclaimer: To be clear: <r2v></r2v> doesn't register you to vote, and we don't approve your application. Your county does that when they receive and process it. We're not your county and not the government <blue>—</blue> we only make it easier to get your completed application to the office that can add you to the voter rolls.
solutionsReady2vote.funding: It's free, run as a civic effort and funded by donations from people who want to make it easier for others to get their application to their county.

solutionsHotline.metaDescription: Scheduling and workforce management by B-59 for civic and public-interest teams: hand-pick a few times and share one link instead of exposing your whole calendar, then run shifts, coverage and hours in the same place. Visit hotlinecal.com.
solutionsHotline.ogDescription: Built by B-59. Share a few times, not your whole calendar — then run the rota, coverage and hours in the same product. Works with Google, Outlook, Apple iCloud or any ICS feed. Visit hotlinecal.com.
solutionsHotline.tagline: Pick a time. Run the week. Count the hours.
solutionsHotline.intro1: Civic and public-interest teams keep sensitive things on their calendars. You shouldn't have to hand over the whole thing just to get a meeting on the books <blue>—</blue> so with Hotline you hand-pick a few times, share one link, and the other person taps one. No account for them, no calendar wall for you, no week of back-and-forth.
solutionsHotline.intro2: That was the wedge. What grew around it is the calendar those teams run the rest of the week from <blue>—</blue> and, for the organizations among them, the rota too: shifts, coverage, hours and cost, in the same product that books the meetings.
solutionsHotline.diff1Body: The host offers a short list of times instead of publishing full availability. For teams whose calendars are a public record — or opposition research — that is the whole point.
solutionsHotline.diff2Strong: Works with the calendar you already keep.
solutionsHotline.diff2Body: Google, Outlook, Apple iCloud, or anything that publishes an ICS feed. Hotline connects to each one directly and labels every busy block with where it came from.
solutionsHotline.diff3Strong: One link, one tap, no account.
solutionsHotline.diff3Body: The other person picks a time from their phone, in their own timezone. Every link is single-use and re-checked at the moment of booking, so a slot can't go twice.
solutionsHotline.diff4Strong: Priced per organization, not per seat.
solutionsHotline.diff4Body: One person is free, with nothing metered. Above that the bill is per organization with unlimited seats — charging by the head is a strange way to bill a team that runs on volunteers, fellows, and people who schedule twice a year.
solutionsHotline.orgHeading: When the calendar isn't only yours
solutionsHotline.orgIntro: Campaigns, mutual aid groups and small nonprofits don't only book meetings <blue>—</blue> they run a rota. Hotline does that in the same place, so the shift schedule isn't a second tool with a second login and a second copy of everyone's name.
solutionsHotline.org1Strong: Build the week as a draft.
solutionsHotline.org1Body: Shifts stay invisible until you publish them, so next month can be worked out in front of people without landing half-formed on anyone's calendar.
solutionsHotline.org2Strong: The people you schedule don't need accounts.
solutionsHotline.org2Body: Add a name. Add an email later, if they want their shifts on their own calendar. Bring a roster in from a spreadsheet and take one back out.
solutionsHotline.org3Strong: Read coverage instead of counting it.
solutionsHotline.org3Body: Who's on, and which days nobody is — as a view of the week rather than a tally you assemble by hand.
solutionsHotline.org4Strong: Hours and cost, straight from the shifts.
solutionsHotline.org4Body: Worked time is reviewed and signed off before it counts as money, then comes out by week or by month as a printable invoice. Admins see the cost; everyone else sees their own hours.
solutionsHotline.why1: Civic and public-interest teams' calendars are sensitive <blue>—</blue> they hold meetings, plans, and people that aren't anyone else's business. Most scheduling tools answer “when are you free?” by publishing the answer, which is exactly the wrong default for this kind of work.
solutionsHotline.why2: So we built the opposite, and then kept going. The teams using it didn't want a booking link bolted to the side of their week <blue>—</blue> they wanted the week itself: the meetings, the shifts, and the hours those shifts add up to, without paying by the person for the privilege.

solutionsTravisCountyVdr.metaDescription: A civic project by B-59. We rebuilt the Travis County Voter Registration Toolkit — the resource hub for Volunteer Deputy Registrars — migrating a legacy site into a fast, accessible, installable web app.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.ogDescription: Built by B-59. A modern, accessible rebuild of the Travis County Voter Registration Toolkit for Volunteer Deputy Registrars.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.heading: Travis County VDR Toolkit
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.intro1: The Travis County Voter Registration Toolkit is the resource hub for (VDRs) — the trained volunteers who register their neighbors and help keep Travis County over 90% registered. It gathers the training, programs, events, and materials a VDR needs in one place.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.intro2: The program had outgrown its original website. <brand></brand> rebuilt it from the ground up: we migrated every page of the legacy site into a fast, accessible, installable web app, and organized the content so the office can keep it current without touching code.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.item1: Migrated the full content library and restructured it as typed data — so editing a page means editing content, not markup.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.item2: Designed a calm, non-partisan civic identity in Travis County navy and Texas gold, built on our shared civic design system.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.item3: Built to accessibility, with a published accessibility statement.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.item4: Shipped it as a — installable to a phone's home screen and usable offline.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.item5: Recovered and curated the program's original artwork and infographics, and documented a clear media and content hand-off.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.why1: Travis County approached us to redesign the Toolkit and turn it into a mobile-first experience <blue>—</blue> something VDRs could actually use in the field, on a phone, while they're registering voters. The original site worked at a desk but not on the ground, which is where most of the work happens.
solutionsTravisCountyVdr.why2: So we rebuilt it mobile-first and installable, and restructured the content so the training, programs, and materials a VDR needs are a tap away wherever they are <blue>—</blue> and so the office can keep it current without touching code.

solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.metaDescription: A client project by B-59. The campaign site for Voter Registration Palooza 2026 — thousands of volunteer-run registration events across Texas before the October 5 deadline. Four bilingual pages and two counts the organizers keep in a spreadsheet.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.ogDescription: Built by B-59. The campaign site for a statewide push to register Texans before the deadline — four pages in English and Spanish, and counts that update from a spreadsheet.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.heading: Voter Registration Palooza
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.intro1: Voter Registration Palooza 2026 is 's push to hold thousands of volunteer-run registration events across Texas in the last days before the October 5 deadline. An event is whatever a deputized volunteer can carry: a table on a street corner, a clipboard outside a theater, a chair in a front yard.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.intro2: <brand></brand> built the site the campaign runs on. Four pages in English and Spanish, two counts the organizers keep in a spreadsheet, and a list of who else is in — live within a week of the brief, and edited since without a deploy.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.item1: Gave each page one question to answer: what the Palooza is, how to get certified as a Deputy Voter Registrar, what the law allows at a table, and who else has signed on. Nobody browses a campaign site in the week before a deadline.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.item2: Wired the running counts and the endorser list to the campaign's own spreadsheets — to change a number or add a name. The endorser list reads its sheet through the Sheets API, so an edit shows up in about ten seconds.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.item3: Designed the failure so a visitor never meets it. A sheet that is missing, unshared, or malformed renders zeros and a written empty state instead of an error. The site does not explain our plumbing to a volunteer.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.item4: Built it in from the first commit, with a test that fails the build when the two catalogs drift apart. Dates are stored once and formatted in the reader's language, so moving a deadline is one line and it is right in both.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.item5: Reproduced the Texas political advertising disclosure verbatim and left it untranslated — it is prescribed language, not copy. The pages carrying eligibility law say in Spanish that the English is authoritative, and link it.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.item6: Pinned the palette's contrast with a test that reads the color tokens out of the stylesheet, and checked the site where the volunteers are: 375px wide, 44px targets, no sideways scroll.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.why1: A registration deadline is a hard edge <blue>—</blue> the work is worth nothing on October 6. Everything the site had to do, it had to do for someone reading on a phone, standing up, with a week left: find the training, learn what is legal at the table, and sign up. So it is four pages, and the numbers move without anyone waiting on us.
solutionsVoterRegistrationPalooza.why2: It is a PAC's site and it is partisan on purpose. That is the client's message, and our job is to make it land rather than to add ours <blue>—</blue> what we bring is the part that is the same on every civic project we take. The law stated accurately. Spanish treated as a language rather than a switch. The whole thing legible on the phone it will actually be read on.

brandPhilosophy.metaDescription: How B-59 approaches brand design. A brand is a set of decisions about how an organization shows up — clarity before polish, restraint as strategy, systems built to be used, and neutrality by default. For campaigns, committees, firms, and institutions where trust is the whole game.
brandPhilosophy.ogDescription: A brand is not a logo. It's a set of decisions about how an organization shows up. How B-59 designs brands for campaigns, committees, firms, and institutions where trust is the whole game.
brandPhilosophy.heading: Brand Design Philosophy
brandPhilosophy.intro: A brand is not a logo. It's the set of decisions an organization makes about how it shows up <blue>—</blue> what it says, what it withholds, and whether the two match. We design brands for organizations that operate where trust is the whole game: campaigns, committees, firms, and institutions that can't afford to look like everyone else, or to look like they're hiding something.
brandPhilosophy.clarityBody: A brand should make the work easier to understand, not harder. We start with what you do and who depends on it, then design outward. Polish is the last 10 percent <blue>—</blue> it matters, but only once the thing underneath is clear.
brandPhilosophy.restraintBody: The temptation is always to add: more color, more motion, more message. We subtract. In high-stakes contexts <blue>—</blue> a campaign in its final weeks, a firm in front of a jury, a committee under scrutiny <blue>—</blue> restraint reads as confidence. The work should look like it knows what it is.
brandPhilosophy.builtBody: A brand lives in the hands of people who aren't designers <blue>—</blue> staff, volunteers, counsel, a comms director at 11pm. We design systems that hold up when we're not in the room: clear rules, real files, and no guesswork. A brand that can only be applied by the people who made it isn't finished.
brandPhilosophy.alignedBody: We work with progressives <blue>—</blue> campaigns, committees, unions, and advocacy organizations on the left, along with the public institutions whose work serves the same end. Within that, the craft is making your message land rather than inserting ours: we bring judgment about what will read as credible to the people you need to reach.

brandPortfolio.ogDescription: Selected brand design work for campaigns, PACs, law firms, and coalitions. Identity systems and collateral built for high-stakes, high-trust work.
brandPortfolio.heading: Selected <blue>work</blue>
brandPortfolio.intro: Brand design for organizations where trust is the whole game <blue>—</blue> political campaigns, PACs, law firms, and advocacy coalitions. Identity systems, brand refreshes, and the field-ready collateral that carries them.
brandPortfolio.disclaimer: Representative engagements; client details anonymized. Named references and full case studies available on request.
brandPortfolio.closingBody: Curious how we'd approach your brand? Read the <link></link> behind the work, or get in touch.
brandPortfolio.item1Result: Logo, color, and a volunteer-ready collateral system deployed across canvassing, mail, and digital — coherent from yard sign to ad.
brandPortfolio.item2Result: Naming, mark, and a messaging framework that stayed disciplined across a multi-race spend.
brandPortfolio.item3Result: Repositioned a litigation firm with a restrained identity and a typographic system built to hold up on the record.
brandPortfolio.item4Result: A neutral, durable mark and palette for a coalition that needed to read as credible to both sides of the aisle.
brandPortfolio.item5Result: A flexible system that kept a slate visually coherent without erasing what made each candidate distinct.
brandPortfolio.item6Result: A wordmark and a short, usable brand guide built for a small team to run on its own.
brandPortfolio.quote1: They gave us something that looked like it had been there for years — steady, serious, and easy for our whole team to actually use.
brandPortfolio.quote2: Restraint was the point. The brand made us look like we knew exactly what we were doing, because by then we did.

merch.intro: Stickers, shirts and print we design for the groups we work with. A brand has to survive being stuck to a laptop or worn to a meeting <blue>—</blue> this is where it gets tested.
merch.stickerBlurb: A die-cut sticker for the club's members. Pflugerville's silent Pf, set in rodeo-poster lettering with a lone star above and below, weathered like it has been on the truck a while. Union printed.

merch.more: More as clients clear them for the page.
